questions.correct: A blueprint that describes how something is built
wrong: The actual object that is built from a plan
A single number stored somewhere in memory
A wire running from the hub to a motor
questions.explain: A class is a blueprint; the object is the actual "room" Java builds from it. Drivebase is the plan; new Drivebase(...) makes a real one.

questions.correct: The actual thing built from a class blueprint
wrong: The blueprint itself, before anything is built
A single button on the driver's gamepad
A telemetry line printed on the screen
questions.explain: An object is what Java builds from the class — like a room built from a blueprint. You make one with new, e.g. new Drivebase(hardwareMap).

questions.q: What two kinds of things does a class hold?
questions.correct: Fields (what it owns) and methods (what it does)
wrong: Imports (what it needs) and comments only
Buttons (its inputs) and wires (its outputs)
Wheels (its parts) and batteries (its power)
questions.explain: A class has fields (data it owns, like its motors) and methods (things it can do, like driveFieldCentric). Together they make a working subsystem.

questions.correct: Set up the object once, finding hardware and starting state
wrong: Run every loop to keep moving the motors
Print telemetry values out to the Driver Hub screen every loop
Reverse the direction of a motor mid-match
questions.explain: The constructor runs once when the object is built. Its job is to find hardware (from hardwareMap) and set the starting state — not to run every loop.

questions.correct: Exactly the same as the class
wrong: Always the single word main
Always the single word build
Any name that you like
questions.explain: The constructor is named exactly after its class (Drivebase's constructor is Drivebase). It also has no return type, not even void.

questions.q: What does "private" do to a field?
questions.correct: Hides it so only that class can touch it
wrong: Shares it with every other class freely
Makes it run a little bit faster on every single loop
Prints it automatically to the telemetry
questions.explain: private is like wiring sealed inside the wall — only the subsystem can touch its motors. That keeps bugs local, since only one place drives them.

questions.q: What does "public" mean for a method?
questions.correct: Any outside code is allowed to call it
wrong: Only the class itself is allowed to call it
It runs all by itself on every loop
It can never be called from anywhere
questions.explain: public is a door everyone can use — outside code (like the OpMode) calls public methods such as driveFieldCentric(...). private is sealed inside.

questions.q: Why hide motors as private inside a subsystem?
questions.correct: So only one place drives them, keeping bugs local
wrong: So the drive motors spin about twice as fast
So the robot's battery lasts a lot longer
So the telemetry updates all by itself
questions.explain: If only the subsystem can touch its motors, there's exactly one place to look when something's wrong. That's encapsulation — it keeps bugs from spreading.

questions.q: What does the Robot class do?
questions.correct: Builds each subsystem once and coordinates them all
wrong: Replaces every subsystem with one giant file
Stores the driver's all-time high score
Charges the robot's battery between matches
questions.explain: Robot.java builds each subsystem once and acts as the coordinator. The OpMode makes one Robot and talks to it instead of wiring everything itself.

questions.correct: Its update() never runs, so it never moves
wrong: The whole program refuses to build
The robot's battery drains twice as fast
The robot starts spinning in a circle
questions.explain: The scheduler only calls update() on subsystems in its list. Forget to add one and its update() never runs — the mechanism just sits there dead.

questions.q: After refactoring, the run loop shrinks to about...
questions.correct: robot.update() and one clean drive call
wrong: fifty long lines of tangled motor math
a single telemetry line and nothing else
nothing at all, since it is now empty
questions.explain: With subsystems, the loop becomes clean: robot.update() advances every subsystem, then one line like robot.drive.driveFieldCentric(...). The mess moved into classes.

questions.q: Why do pro teams split code into subsystems?
questions.correct: Different people can work on different files at once
wrong: It makes the robot drive a great deal faster
The rules require the code to be one file
It saves a lot of space on the battery
questions.explain: Subsystems in separate files let one person build the Drivebase while another builds the Intake — no stepping on each other's code, and easier to debug.

questions.q: A constructor has what return type?
questions.correct: None at all, not even void
wrong: Always the type int
Always the type boolean
Always the type double
questions.explain: Constructors have NO return type — not even void. They're special methods, named after the class, that set up a new object.

questions.q: A private field can be reached from the OpMode by...
questions.correct: Calling a public method on the subsystem
wrong: Reading the field directly by its name
Rewiring the motor's cable by hand
Adding one more telemetry line for it
questions.explain: Private fields are sealed inside, so outside code goes through public methods. That's the point — a controlled door instead of reaching into the wiring.

questions.q: What does the constructor use to find its motors?
wrong: The telemetry object it prints to
The gamepad1 stick and button inputs
The battery voltage on the hub
questions.explain: The constructor takes a HardwareMap and calls hardwareMap.get(...) to find each motor by name. That's why you pass hardwareMap when building the subsystem.
